title: How a tile gets its data

promises.promise: One GraphQL endpoint, generated from the same schema as the database. A tile sends a query naming exactly the fields and connected things it wants, gets the rows, then receives changes as subscriptions over the websocket.
There is one definition of the data, and no hand-written reads.
A tile names exactly the fields and connected things it wants.
A page reads with one API call, backed by a fixed small number of SQL statements that does not grow with the number of rows, with visibility checked for whoever is asking.
After the first rows, loom sends only what changed.
A query names a table from the model and the fields it wants. Any app's tile asks the same way.
The connection knows the caller from its session or token.
The labels on each row decide whether this caller gets it.
A new inbox item reaches an open Inbox tile as a change.

The endpoint is generated from the same Drizzle schema as the tables, so there is one definition of the data and no hand-written reads. GraphQL is a widely used standard with ready-made tools on both ends.

Loom handles the request in one API call using a fixed small number of sane SQL statements, independent of the number of rows. Several batched statements are fine. Filtering and visibility checks happen in the database.
After the first rows, changes arrive as subscriptions over the websocket. A tile never asks again for what it already has.
The tables on every page of this site are one schema, defined once. A query is written against that schema, so nothing is stored as a bundle the database cannot look inside.
a Checked in the query. The visibility check runs inside the query, for whoever is asking. A caller never receives a row it may not see, or that row's changes.

b The rule. Household owners can read these records. Anyone else sees what is in their projects, plus what belongs to agents they own. Only the participating member can read their private conversation with an agent.
c Installed means trusted. The check is for callers from outside. Loom's own parts never ask each other for permission.
machine_reads Diagnostic request metadata for the machine owner’s history. The answer text is never stored here.
migrations The list of changes already made to the database's shape, so each is applied once.
operation_results The result of each recent write, kept 30 days, so a retry after a dropped connection returns the same answer and nothing happens twice.
notification_queue Notifications waiting to be sent to each device, and whether each arrived.

bridge_raw_events Events exactly as Discord and Slack sent them, kept until they are turned into incoming messages: up to a day for one that cannot be read yet, and an hour from arrival once it has been. The one place loom stores something it does not look inside.
bridge_resume Where each Discord connection left off, so it can pick up after a restart, and the credential it was made under.
bridge_send_parts The id the app gave each posted part of a reply, in order. A long reply goes out in parts; these say how far it got and which outside messages are the bot's own.
bridge_file_messages Which messages carried each kept Slack or Discord attachment. A file shared in two messages is listed under both and kept once.
bridge_send_files The files a post carries, kept only until the post is sent, dismissed or left in doubt.
terminal_credentials The machine and member an enrolled credential may report terminal sessions for.
terminal_sessions The private Comms thread and parent job for a harness session on a member’s machine.
terminal_runs The parent job, run identifier and last transcript revision for each observed terminal run.

conversation_sessions A model program's own record of a conversation, sealed, kept between runs so the next one picks up where the last left off. One for a conversation and program; nothing but the next run reads it. It is erased when the household's keep time has passed since it was started, however often it was saved since; the next run then starts over.
secret_write_journal A two-step record between loom and the key holder so a value change interrupted by a crash is finished or undone, never half done.
The real GraphQL websocket carries data after sign-in without protocol errors.
